title: TST: to_csv quotes a bare carriage return (GH#10018)

labels.name: Testing
labels.description: pandas testing functions or related to the test suite

body:
closes #10018

A field containing a bare `\r` written by `to_csv` with the default `lineterminator="\n"` used not to be quoted, so `read_csv` treated the `\r` as a line terminator and split the field across rows. The cause was in CPython's `_csv` writer, which under `QUOTE_MINIMAL` only quoted characters found in the writer's `lineterminator`; it was fixed upstream by CPython gh-67044 (bpo-22855) and backported to 3.11.9 / 3.12.3 / 3.13.0, all within pandas' `requires-python >= 3.11`.

Existing tests cover embedded `\n` and `\r\n` but never a bare `\r`, which is the case reported here, so this adds that regression test and closes the issue. No behavior change.

The issue also proposed changing `read_csv`'s default `lineterminator` to `"\n"`; that is not done here, since auto-detecting `\r` / `\n` / `\r\n` is what makes files written on either platform readable with the defaults.

title: BUG: iloc setitem wrote the wrong cells on a Copy-on-Write referenced frame (GH#65446)

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Internals
labels.description: Related to non-user accessible pandas implementation

body:
Fixes a regression from GH-65864, which is in 3.0.4 and later.

When another object references a `DataFrame`'s values, `BlockManager.setitem` splits the block so only the targeted columns get copied, then re-expresses the caller's column indexer in the new block's coordinates. GH-65864 collapsed any increasing column selection to `slice(None)` and compensated for reordered ones with an array of positions, plus a reshape of the row indexer to `(n, 1)`. Both substitutions change what numpy does: a slice takes the cross product with the row indexer, an array broadcasts against it. So the referenced path could disagree with the unreferenced one in either direction — writing a cross product where the caller asked for an elementwise pairing, or the other way round.

The column indexer now keeps the kind the caller used: an integer stays an integer, a slice stays a slice (reversed if the selection was), anything else stays an array of positions. The row-indexer reshape goes with it — it was independently wrong, turning an intended broadcast into a cross product whenever `np.ix_` had not already run — and so does the `np.squeeze`, which is only correct for `np.ix_` output and can no longer receive any.

Symptoms fixed, all only when another object holds a reference:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame(np.arange(12.0).reshape(4, 3), columns=list("abc"))
ref = df[["a", "b", "c"]]

df.iloc[[2, 0], ::-1] = np.array([100.0, 101.0, 102.0])
# IndexError: shape mismatch: indexing arrays could not be broadcast
#   together with shapes (2,) (3,)

df.iloc[np.array([1, 0]), range(1, -1, -1)] = 99.0
# silently writes 4 cells; without the reference it writes 2

df.loc[np.array([True, False, True, False]), "c":"a":-1] = 99.0
# IndexError: too many indices for array: array is 2-dimensional, but 3 were indexed
```

Verified with a referenced-vs-unreferenced differential — the unreferenced path never enters this code, so it is the oracle. Over 35,728 cases (4 dtypes x 4 frame shapes x 20 row-key spellings x 14 column-key spellings x 7 value shapes, `iloc` and `loc`) `main` diverges in 3,621 and this branch in 0.

Remaining divergences in that sweep are all the empty-indexer family, where an early return skips value validation. That predates GH-65864 and is left alone here.

AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which wrote the fix and tests and ran the differential sweeps; reviewed by me.

title: BUG: HDFStore where-clause with a None operand answered instead of raising (GH#64348)
body:
Follow-up to GH-64348, which switched `BinOp.prune` to pass `Term` objects into its inner `pr()` helper instead of their values, so the helper's `right is None` short-circuit stopped firing. A `where=` clause whose right-hand operand is `None` — reachable whenever an optional query parameter is threaded into the query string — then stopped erroring and started answering: a bool data column returns the rows where it is `False` (`bool(None)` is `False`), datetime64/timedelta64 columns the `NaT` rows, a categorical column 0 rows, and `where="columns == None"` a 0-column frame.

That half is unreleased, but `HDFStore.remove` is not — on 3.0.x the pruned condition collapses to the bare column name, which PyTables evaluates as a boolean mask, so `store.remove(key, where="a == None")` on a bool data column silently deletes the rows where it is `True`. Hence the whatsnew entry names `remove` only.

The guard goes in `BinOp.conform` rather than `convert_value` because it is the first data step of both `ConditionBinOp.evaluate` and `FilterBinOp.evaluate`, so the condition and filter paths are covered in one place. Not cherry-pickable to 3.0.x, where `prune` still short-circuits before `conform`.

title: BUG: DataFrame axis=1 reductions accumulated in each block's own dtype (GH#51474)
body:
Repairs a silent-wrong-answer defect in the block-wise `axis=1` reduction fast path added by GH-65105 (for GH-51474). That PR is unreleased, so the wrong answers never reached users and there is no *Bug fixes* whatsnew entry.

`DataFrame._reduce_axis1` reduced each block in that block's **own** dtype and combined the per-block partials with a numpy ufunc, where the transpose path it replaced reduced in the common dtype of all blocks. On current `main`:

| frame | `axis=1` | `df.T` (correct) |
|---|---|---|
| int64 + float `sum` | `-9.22e18` | `9.22e18` |
| uint64 + float `sum` | `0.5` | `1.84e19` |
| int64 + uint8 `sum` | `4.6e18` (float64) | `4611686018427387906` (int64) |
| float32 + float `sum` | `inf` | `6.0e38` |
| bool + complex64 `mean` | `1.0` | `1+1j` |

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [2**62], "b": [2**62], "c": [0.5]})
df.sum(axis=1)  # -9.223372036854776e+18
df.T.sum()      #  9.223372036854776e+18
```

Compute one cross-block accumulation dtype with `np.result_type`, widen it for `mean` the way `nanmean` does (float64 for int/bool/float16, complex128 for complex), and `astype` each block to it before reducing. `mean` also stops unconditionally casting the combined result to float64, which is what discarded the imaginary part.

`find_common_type` cannot serve as the accumulation dtype here: it returns `object` as soon as a bool block is present, which would switch the fix off for exactly the bool+numeric frames that reach this path.

There **is** an *Other API changes* entry, for a behavior change GH-65105 itself introduced and did not document: these reductions on a bool+numeric mix now return a numeric dtype instead of going through `object`, so an integer `sum` can overflow where Python's arbitrary-precision arithmetic used to keep it exact, and `min`/`max` on a bool+complex mix return a value where they previously raised.

Verified against the transpose oracle over ~247k dtype × shape × method × `skipna` × `min_count` cells, with no value divergence introduced; each of the five families above fails if the fix is reverted.

title: BUG: to_datetime with unit= and an out-of-bounds float returned NaT or raised OverflowError

labels.name: Error Reporting
labels.description: Incorrect or improved errors from pandas

body:
Two ways `to_datetime` with `unit=` mishandled a float outside the int64 domain:

- With `unit="Y"`/`"M"` the int64-domain check sat below the `unit in "YM"` branch, which does its own unchecked `values.astype("M8[Y]")`. A float below `-2**63` clamps to `INT64_MIN`, which *is* the `NaT` sentinel, so `to_datetime(np.array([-1e19]), unit="Y")` silently returned `NaT`.
- A round float in a list or object-dtype argument was cast at the call site in `tslib.pyx`, outside `cast_from_unit`'s `try`/`except`, so `to_datetime([1e30], unit="s")` raised a bare `OverflowError` where the ndarray path raised `OutOfBoundsDatetime`. That one is a 3.0.0 regression from GH-63595.

The bounds check is now a helper called from both branches, each time *after* that branch's own validation, so the "ambiguous non-round float" and "Unrecognized unit" errors keep precedence over it.

Two consequences fall out of doing that: `±inf` with `unit="Y"`/`"M"` now raises `OutOfBoundsDatetime` rather than `ValueError`, matching every other unit; and `unit in "YM"` — substring containment, which also matched `""` and `"YM"` — becomes `unit in ("Y", "M")`, matching the scalar path.

title: BUG: td64 dtype ignored its unit for numbers mixed with timedelta-like objects (GH#68639)
body:
`TimedeltaArray._from_sequence` applied the dtype's unit only when every non-null value was numeric, so a plain number mixed with a timedelta-like object was read as nanoseconds:

```python
>>> pd.Series([pd.Timedelta(1, "s"), 2], dtype="m8[s]")
0   0 days 00:00:01
1   0 days 00:00:00      # want 0 days 00:00:02
dtype: timedelta64[s]
```

`pd.to_timedelta([pd.Timedelta(1, "s"), 2], unit="s")` was already correct. The same held for `np.timedelta64`, `datetime.timedelta` and `offsets.Day` mixed with a number, and for floats.

The gate becomes "apply the unit unless a `str` is present". The `str` carve-out is needed because `array_to_timedelta64` rejects a unit passed alongside string input; matching `to_timedelta`, which raises there, would need a deprecation cycle. The check uses a new Cython helper `lib.has_string_element` instead of the previous `isna()` mask plus `lib.is_integer_float_array`, so it is also cheaper than the gate it replaces on every object-dtype input.

Pre-existing on main; it predates GH-63499 and GH-66180, which introduced the gate being replaced.

title: BUG: ArrowExtensionArray silently truncated a value an integer dtype cannot hold (GH#68638)

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

body:
`pd.Series([1, 2, 3], dtype="int64[pyarrow]").replace(2, 1.5)` returned `[1, 1, 3]` — the replacement landed, truncated toward zero, with no error and no warning. The numpy-backed Series upcasts to float64 and stores 1.5; the masked `Int64` Series raises `TypeError`. Only the arrow-backed one silently corrupted the value.

`ArrowExtensionArray._validate_setitem_value` boxed the value with `pa.scalar(value, type=pa_type)`, which converts unsafely — `pa.scalar(1.5, type=pa.int64())` is `1`. Because that never raised, the block-level machinery above it never engaged and `putmask_inplace` wrote the truncated value. The same boxing pattern appeared a second time in `_fillna`.

This rejects a lossy value in `_validate_setitem_value` with `TypeError`, matching `BaseMaskedArray._validate_setitem_value`, and routes `_fillna` through that same validation. `Series`/`DataFrame` now raise; `Index.where`/`Index.putmask` upcast, since `Index` has no column-dtype contract to protect — both matching the nullable integer dtypes.

The check is a deny-list rather than masked's allow-list on purpose: an allow-list would also turn `arr[0] = "x"` from `ArrowInvalid` into `TypeError`, which is a separate change with its own test fallout.

Adjacent defects found while working on this and deliberately left out: `insert` truncates through `_from_sequence`; `_box_pa_scalar` raises `AttributeError` for a `Timestamp` against a non-matching type; `interpolate`'s linear fast path integer-divides; a dictionary-encoded integer type is not `pa.types.is_integer` and so still truncates.

title: BUG: ops with an iterator raised TypeError instead of treating it as a scalar (GH#31646)

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

body:
closes #31646

Comparison and arithmetic between a pandas object and an iterator — a generator, `iter([...])`, `map`, `filter`, `reversed` — raised `TypeError: object of type 'generator' has no len()` (or `len() of unsized object`), because the op sites gated on `is_list_like(other)` or `lib.is_scalar(other)` and then took a length. NumPy arrays and NumPy-dtype Series already treat an iterator as a scalar.

Two helpers in `pandas/core/ops/common.py` replace those gates across the array and frame op sites:

- `is_listlike_for_op(other)` = `is_list_like(other) and (hasattr(other, "__len__") or has_castable_attr(other))`, replacing `is_list_like`.
- `is_scalar_for_op(other)` = `is_scalar(other) or not (hasattr(other, "__len__") or has_castable_attr(other))`, replacing `lib.is_scalar`. Deliberately not the negation of the first: a sized sequence with `__getitem__` but no `__iter__` is not `is_list_like`, yet NumPy coerces it, so it has to stay element-wise.

Iterators become scalar-like now rather than after a deprecation cycle, because the current behavior is a crash rather than a result worth preserving — and the merged GH-62423 deprecation already says non-standard list-likes become scalar-like in 4.0. Two of the three user-visible changes were silent rather than loud: a `Sparse` dtype and an `ExtensionScalarOpsMixin`-based array consumed a length-matching iterator and computed elementwise, and `ArrowDtype` arithmetic looped forever on an endless one (`ser + itertools.count()`).

Related, not addressed here: GH-62423 (the deprecation this follows), and `where`/`mask`/`__setitem__`, which have the same shape but want the opposite resolution, since `pd.Series(gen)` materializes.

title: BUG avoid parallel read_csv with converters
body:
Closes #68505

### Summary

Prevent the parallel `read_csv` path from being selected when user-defined `converters` are provided.

Converter callables execute in parser worker threads and may be stateful or depend on thread-affine resources. Running them in parallel can therefore change behavior or raise thread-affinity errors compared with the serial path.

### Changes

- Exclude `converters` from `_can_parallelize_csv` eligibility.
- Add a regression test covering the eligibility check.

### Testing

- `git diff --check` passes.
- The focused pytest could not be executed locally because the pandas C extensions are not built in the Windows environment (`pandas._libs.pandas_parser` is unavailable). This is an environment/build limitation rather than a test failure.
